title: Chief Economists Outlook: what bond yields and interest rates tell us about the global economy
gist: WEF's September 2026 Chief Economists Outlook shows sentiment stabilising (share expecting weakening fell from ~90% to under half), but EY's Gregory Daco warns Middle East-driven inflation will push the Fed and others to tighten. He attributes the US 10-year's rise to ~5% (highest since the GFC) to a cyclical oil spark plus structural drivers - fiscal deficits, inflation volatility, AI capex crowding out Treasuries, and central-bank credibility doubts.

insights.claim: In the WEF Chief Economists Outlook (September 2026), the share of chief economists expecting global conditions to weaken fell from about nine in ten in May to a little less than half, with 'stabilising' the dominant sentiment.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Sentiment improvement is mostly base-effect relief after the Middle East war shock, not evidence of a new upswing.
insights.quote: we went from about nine and 10 down to a little less than half
insights.locator: John Letzing: Yeah, so context is very important

insights.claim: Economists appear to be normalising the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea threats as a 'new normal', reading the economy's resilience as grounds for mild optimism despite unresolved energy chokepoints.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Markets/economists may be under-pricing re-escalation risk because adaptation is being mistaken for resolution.
insights.locator: Robin Pomeroy: Is that because the world

insights.claim: EY's Gregory Daco describes the global outlook as resilient but polarised, with geopolitics, tariffs and the AI-led tech revolution pushing different economies in different directions.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Expect widening divergence across countries and sectors rather than a synchronised global cycle.
insights.quote: there is resilience, but there is also polarisation in the face of numerous shocks
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: I think if you look

insights.claim: Although chief economists' headline inflation expectations eased slightly, they expect cost-of-living basics such as food, electricity and transport to keep rising; in September half expected inflation to rise and half expected it to stabilise.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Headline calm masks sticky essentials inflation that keeps central banks on hold-or-hike footing.
insights.quote: half of the chief economist expected inflation to rise and half expecting inflation to stabilise
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: What we are seeing is

insights.claim: Daco expects renewed Middle East tensions, higher commodity prices and supply-chain disruptions to re-accelerate global inflation, with the Fed likely to follow other central banks that have already tightened.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Positioning for a 2026-27 tightening cycle (US, likely UK) rather than cuts.
insights.quote: It's likely the Fed will follow suit with some tightening of its monetary policy.
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: What we are seeing is

insights.claim: The combination of higher input and consumer prices alongside higher rates and cost of capital creates a hard-to-manage duality for growth heading into 2027.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Stagflationary mix is negative for margins and rate-sensitive equities simultaneously.
insights.quote: that duality is something we have to monitor very closely in the next few months as we navigate into 2027
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: What we are seeing is

insights.claim: Negative supply shocks from the Middle East, Ukraine and renewed US tariffs are crystallising into higher inflation and thus a structurally higher interest-rate environment.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Supply-side inflation limits how far central banks can ease even if demand slows.
insights.quote: all of those are leading to a higher interest rate environment because they're crystallising into higher inflation
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: I think one thing to realise

insights.claim: The US 10-year Treasury yield hit about 5%, its highest since the 2007-09 global financial crisis, a psychologically important level because the 10-year prices corporate borrowing, auto loans and mortgages globally.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A sustained 5% 10-year resets the global cost of capital and equity discount rates.
insights.quote: a 5% 10-year bond yield is the highest we would have seen since before COVID, you have to go back to the great financial crisis of 2007, 2009
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: So before we go into the 5% mark

insights.claim: Daco separates a cyclical spark (Middle East oil shock and hike expectations) from four structural drivers of higher long-term yields: post-COVID fiscal deficits and debt, inflation volatility that makes central-bank moves hard to price, AI pulling private capital away from Treasuries, and doubts over central-bank credibility.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Even if the cyclical spark fades, term premium stays elevated; don't expect a full yield round-trip.
insights.quote: These factors are not going away.
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: I think there are a few factors

insights.claim: The AI capex boom is crowding out demand for government debt: investors weigh high expected AI returns against Treasuries, diverting capital to data centres and semiconductor facilities, while central-bank balance-sheet runoff further reduces sovereign bond demand.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: AI investment is a channel for higher sovereign yields, linking tech capex to rates risk.
insights.quote: They can either invest in Treasury bonds or they can invest in AI.
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: Yes, that's a big part of it

insights.claim: US Treasury interventions - supporting the Japanese yen to stem Treasury selling and larger debt buybacks resembling an 'Operation Twist' swap of short for long duration - signal administration discomfort with high rates and may be exacerbating investor doubts.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Official yield suppression attempts can backfire as a credibility signal; watch for steeper front end.
insights.quote: Those combinations of interventions are signalling to private sector investments some discomfort from the administration
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: I think there are a few factors

insights.claim: If the Middle East conflict ended and oil flows resumed, inflation and inflation expectations would fall and central banks would likely hold, lowering long-term rates - but structural upward pressures on yields would remain.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A peace deal is a tactical duration rally, not a regime change in yields.
insights.quote: the structural factors that are still putting upward pressure on long-term government bond yields are still going to be present
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: I think one thing to realise

insights.claim: Bond markets act as a final reality check: when investors doubt a government's repayment ability or a central bank's inflation resolve, they demand a risk premium, as seen in the 2022 UK episode, often accompanied by private-sector pullback and equity corrections.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Unrealistic budgets are the trigger to watch for sovereign yield spikes and equity drawdowns.
insights.quote: It does function as a reality check for the cost of that debt
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: In a way, yes

insights.claim: Economies with deep markets, institutional credibility, rule of law, moderate debt and small deficits pay lower rates, while smaller, geopolitically volatile, fiscally weak economies face very high rates usually alongside higher inflation.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Sovereign spread dispersion should widen along credibility and fiscal lines.
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: Yeah, you can see that

insights.claim: Persistent large deficits create a debt-interest snowball that can force inflation and tightening; Daco hopes the near-5% 10-year forces policymakers to curb healthcare and ageing spending and shore up the tax base.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Fiscal consolidation is hoped for, not expected - timing of any bond-market-forced adjustment is unknown.
insights.quote: you have a snowball effect there that can lead to higher inflation and force central banks to tighten monetary policy
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: I would hope so

insights.claim: Mortgage rates for US homebuyers are already much higher than six months ago because both 10-year and 30-year yields have risen, but because most debt is fixed, the impact on activity filters gradually through marginal buyers and refinancing.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Housing and new-borrowing-dependent sectors feel it first; aggregate drag builds with a lag.
insights.quote: It affects only the marginal buyer
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: I mean, in some cases

insights.claim: Higher 10-year yields raise auto-loan, mortgage and corporate bond costs, likely leading firms to pull back on investment and hiring intentions.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Watch capex and hiring surveys for second-round effects of the yield spike.
insights.quote: perhaps lead to a pullback in investment intentions and in hiring intentions
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: So essentially, when you think

insights.claim: Some 79% of chief economists see likely local community pushback against data-centre expansion.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Permitting/local opposition is a real constraint on AI infrastructure timelines.
insights.quote: about 79% of the chief economists seeing some likely pushback to data centre expansion from local communities
insights.locator: John Letzing: Indeed. And we should note

insights.claim: Daco argues the first phase of any technological revolution, AI included, is capex- and infrastructure-intensive, straining resources and generating inflation; disinflationary productivity gains only arrive later with skills and diffusion.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: AI is near-term inflationary, supporting higher rates now, with disinflation a later payoff.
insights.quote: in the first phase of a technological revolution, there are inflationary pressures
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: I think it will have to be

insights.claim: While AI should ultimately lift productivity and business investment, its initial phase will create labour displacement, energy strains and risk of asset-market overappreciation, requiring proactive public-private management.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Expect AI winners and losers plus bubble risk; policy will shape externalities.
insights.quote: this is just not going to be everybody wins all the time
insights.locator: Gregory Daco: I think in general
